summary.text: pH is a logarithmic scale used to say how acidic or basic a water-based solution is.
At 25 °C a pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, and exactly 7 is neutral, the same as pure water.
Acidic solutions have more hydrogen ions and so a lower pH, and pH can be measured with a glass electrode and meter or a color-changing indicator.

facts.label: Letter p
facts.value: Its exact original meaning is disputed

items.prompt: Pure water is heated well above 25 °C. What happens to the pH value that counts as neutral?

options.label: It falls below 7
It stays fixed at exactly 7
It rises above 7
It no longer means anything

items.explain: The neutral pH depends on temperature and is lower than 7 when the temperature rises above 25 °C.

items.prompt: A kitchen cleaner is basic and vinegar is acidic. Which one should read the lower pH?

options.label: The cleaner, since bases carry more hydrogen ions
The vinegar, since acids carry more hydrogen ions
Both read the same, since pH ignores hydrogen ions
Neither, since pH only applies to pure water

items.explain: Acidic solutions have higher concentrations of hydrogen cations and measure lower pH values than basic ones.

items.prompt: A friend says it is settled that the p in pH stands for 'potential'. What is the accurate reply?

options.label: It stands for the Latin pondus, as Sørensen wrote
It stands for 'power', confirmed in Danish records
It stands for the French puissance and nothing else
Its exact meaning is still disputed, since Sørensen never explained it

items.explain: Sørensen did not explain the p, and several readings such as power or potential remain possible. The Latin readings are not supported by his writings.

items.prompt: A lab report gives only a solution's pH. The number is built from the concentration of which ion?

options.label: Hydroxide ions, OH⁻
Chloride ions, Cl⁻
Hydrogen ions, H⁺
Sodium ions, Na⁺

items.explain: pH is the negative decimal logarithm of the H⁺ ion concentration. pOH is the matching quantity for OH⁻.

items.prompt: A citrus company wanted a quicker way to test the pH of lemons as they were picked. What did this request lead to?

options.label: A professor's first electronic method for measuring pH
The first definition of pH as a letter and a number
A method that replaced meters with only paper strips
The idea that the p stands for power

items.explain: Sunkist's request led Arnold Beckman, a Caltech professor, to invent the first electronic method of measuring pH.

items.prompt: A student says pH is always between 0 and 14. Which solution shows that range is only the common convention?

options.label: A very dilute strong base, which can read below 0
A very concentrated strong acid, which can read below 0
Pure water kept cold, which can read above 14
Any solution at 25 °C, which can read below 0

items.explain: The 0 to 14 range is commonly given, but very concentrated strong acids can go below 0 and very concentrated strong bases above 14.

paragraphs.heading: What pH tells you
paragraphs.text: pH is a logarithmic scale for saying how acidic or basic a water-based solution is. The more hydrogen ions (H⁺) a solution carries, the more acidic it is, and the lower its pH reads. Chemists track those ions as a molar concentration, written [H⁺] and counted in moles per litre. In modern usage the letter p means "the negative decimal logarithm of", so pH is the negative decimal logarithm of the H⁺ concentration, and pOH is the same thing for hydroxide ions (OH⁻).

paragraphs.heading: Acidic, basic and neutral
paragraphs.text: At 25 °C, anything below pH 7 counts as acidic and anything above 7 counts as basic. A reading of exactly 7 is neutral: H⁺ and OH⁻ ions are present in equal amounts, just as in pure water. That neutral mark moves with temperature, sliding under 7 when the solution is warmer than 25 °C. People often quote the scale as running from 0 to 14, yet very concentrated strong acids can fall below zero and very concentrated strong bases can climb past 14.

paragraphs.heading: A letter nobody can explain
paragraphs.text: The Danish chemist Søren Sørensen brought in the idea in 1909 while working at the Carlsberg Laboratory. In 1924 it was reworked into today's pH so that it fit measurements made with electrochemical cells. Sørensen never said why he picked the letter p, and its meaning is still argued over. It may come from the French, German or Danish word for "power" (puissance, Potenz, potens), or it may mean "potential". Some books claim a Latin origin, but his own writings do not back that up.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: pH can be read with a glass electrode wired to a pH meter, or with an indicator dye that changes color. The precise method, set out in the international standard ISO 31-8, builds a galvanic cell: a reference electrode and an electrode that responds to hydrogen ions stand in the same solution, and the electromotive force between them is measured. The cell is first filled with a solution whose hydrogen ion level is already known, then with the unknown one. The gap between the two readings is proportional to pH. In practice a glass electrode stands in for the clumsy hydrogen electrode.

paragraphs.heading: An agreed yardstick
paragraphs.text: Every pH reading traces back to a set of standard solutions whose values are fixed by international agreement. Those primary values are found with a concentration cell that compares a hydrogen electrode against a standard electrode, such as one made of silver chloride.

paragraphs.heading: Why the number matters
paragraphs.text: Knowing pH is useful in chemistry, agronomy, medicine, water treatment and many other fields. While studying bacterial metabolism, Dr. Clark found that what affects the growth of bacteria is the intensity of an acid, meaning its hydrogen-ion concentration. Older methods only measured how much acid was there. He and his colleagues worked out accurate ways to measure hydrogen-ion concentration, and these displaced the rough titration methods used in biology labs around the world. In 1934, Arnold Beckman of the California Institute of Technology built the first electronic way to measure pH, answering a request from the citrus grower Sunkist for a quicker test of the lemons picked in its nearby orchards.
